hints: You want small letters as early as possible. When a smaller letter arrives, you could throw away a bigger letter you kept earlier, but only if that bigger letter still shows up later in s.
Greedy monotonic stack of chosen letters, plus each letter's last index and a boolean array saying which letters are already in the stack.

1. Record last[c], the last index of each letter.
  2. For each index i with letter c: if c is already in the stack, skip it.
  3. While the top is bigger than c and last[top] > i, pop the top and mark it as not used.
  4. Push c and mark it used.
  5. The stack, bottom to top, is the answer.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Generate every subsequence that has each distinct letter exactly once and keep the smallest.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Build the answer one letter at a time: pick the smallest letter whose position still leaves all other needed letters after it, then repeat on the rest.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: One pass with a stack: pop a larger letter on top when it appears again later, and never push a letter that is already kept.

explain: For s = "dbcadc" the last indices are d:5, b:1, c:4, a:3. Push d. At b, d is bigger and appears later, so pop d; push b. Push c. At a, c is bigger and appears later (index 4), so pop it; b is bigger but never appears again, so it stays; push a. Push d. At the final c, d is bigger but this was its last copy, so it stays; push c. Result "badc". The rule keeps every letter available: we only discard a letter when another copy is still ahead.
recognize: Keep each distinct letter once, preserve order, and get the lexicographically smallest result → greedy monotonic stack with last occurrences.
